newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to arrest Hanbo heir, seize family fortune.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to arrest Hanbo heir, seize family fortune.

text.p: After bringing to trial the patriach of South Korea's Hanbo Group, whose steel unit collapsed in a loans scandal, prosecutors on Thursday said they would seek to arrest his son and seize the family fortune.
Prosecutors have so far uncovered family assets of more than 300 billion won ($337 million) and are digging for more hidden wealth, a prosecution official said.

Chung Tae-soo, patriach of South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate whose flagship steelmaking company folded under debts of $5.8 billion in January, went on trial for bribery along with nine other people this month.
His son, Chung Bo-keun, is group chairman.
"Prosecutors questioning Hanbo Chairman Chung Bo-keun have decided to seek an arrest warrant for him," a prosecution official said.
He said investigators were still probing the younger Chung for evidence to charge him with embezzlement.

"Prosecutors will continue to dig further to find out whether there is other hidden wealth held by the family," he said. "We are determined to end the bad practice of the past when businessmen survived even when their businesses collapsed."
Hanbo Steel's failure revealed a web of corruption and influence-peddling involving top bankers and politicians that allowed the company to secure loans far in excess of its ability to repay them.
On trial with Chung Tae-soo are a former cabinet minister, aides to President Kim Young-sam and bank executives.
Thursday's announcement was the first breakthrough in the case since state prosecutors reopened their probe last Friday after replacing the lead investigator.
An earlier investigation, which brought the elder Chung to trial, was dismissed by opposition parties as a whitewash that had failed to bring to justice the leading actors.
In particular, the opposition is demanding a thorough investigation into the role played by president Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul.

Prosecutors are now looking into what they call rumours that Kim Hyun-chul took a 200 billion-won ($225 million) kickback linked to a German equipment purchase by Hanbo Steel. Last Friday they raided the home and offices of a close associate of Kim Hyun-chul looking for evidence.
On Wednesday, prosecutors questioned two bankers in connection with the loans-for-kickbacks scandal.
One was a branch manager of Korea First Bank, Hanbo's main creditor, and the other an executive at the Commercial Bank of Korea, which also lent heavily to the company.
President Kim apologised last month for the Hanbo furore and reshuffled his cabinet. The junior Kim issued a statement saying he was ready to receive punishment if he had done wrong.
Kim Hyun-chul is scheduled to testify before a National Assembly hearing on Hanbo in April, which will be broadcast live on television. Parliament began a 45-day special investigation last Friday.
